extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematical researchers, teachers, students, and developers of mathematical AI interested in heuristics and conjecture evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: A rubric describing how to evaluate and produce mathematical work that relies on plausible (inductive/analogical/abductive) reasoning as well as deductive proof; covers what counts as good inductive evidence, use of analogy, generalization/specialization heuristics, hygiene of conjecture-making, and implications for AI-generated mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish demonstrative and plausible reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical work involves two distinct logics: demonstrative (deductive proof, certain) and plausible reasoning (inductive, analogical, abductive guessing — uncertain but indispensable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate pieces of work on both axes: assess correctness and rigor of proof, and separately assess the plausibility-evidence that motivated conjectures. Avoid collapsing conjecture-level arguments into proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive evidence robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive (evidential) support for a conjecture should come from a non-trivial number of checked cases chosen with variety; lack of exceptions after substantial search increases plausibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good practice: check many cases, vary the types/sizes of cases (not only consecutive small ones), document which cases were checked, and report if negative cases were sought. Bad practice: presenting a few trivial checks as if they suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly note analogies to known cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical work that explicitly notes its analogies to known cases is more comprehensible and generative than one that hides them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the analogous setting(s) and how the analogy informs conjecture formation or strategy. Use analogy as an explanatory and heuristic device, not as implicit evidence masked by formal language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use generalization as a heuristic move
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalization: posing a problem in wider terms may make it easier or reveal deeper structure; using generalization is a plausible-reasoning move.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately attempt broader formulations when stuck; explain why the generalization is expected to help. Avoid treating generalization as merely ornament; show how it guided reasoning or led to progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specialization as a heuristic move
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialization: trying the simplest/special case can illuminate the general problem and suggest patterns to be generalized back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report investigations of special cases and how they informed conjectures or proofs. Do not dismiss special-case exploration as embarrassing; document its role in discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of consequence (confirmation increases plausibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A implies B and B is observed true, this increases the plausibility of A (but does not prove A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how many and what kinds of consequences were verified; stronger confirmations come from consequences that were not expected a priori.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of incompatible consequence (refutation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A implies B and B is false, then A is refuted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively seek incompatible consequences as a method for refutation; negative evidence is decisive and should be reported when found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of one of many possible consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When A entails many consequences C1, C2, …, verifying one or more of them increases plausibility of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer verifying consequences that are independent and informative rather than trivial corollaries; document the range of consequences considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successful prediction as strong confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: If A predicts a previously-unknown phenomenon and that phenomenon is later observed, this strongly increases A's plausibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight genuine predictions (not retrodictions) that were later confirmed; such successes are particularly persuasive evidence for conjectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility by analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: A conjecture gains plausibility if a similar conjecture in an analogous setting was true; analogy transfers some degree of support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the depth and limits of the analogy; state what structural features are shared and where the analogy might break down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to a previously settled case
rubrics_metrics.description: If A can be reduced to B and B is known, then A becomes plausible (and may be nearly proved depending on the reduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document reductions carefully: clarify assumptions and whether the reduction preserves required hypotheses. Reduction increases confidence more when the target (B) is well-established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausible-reasoning hygiene (multiple confirmations and refutation-seeking)
rubrics_metrics.description: A research program should be judged by its plausible-reasoning hygiene: are conjectures supported by multiple independent confirmations? Have possible refutations been actively sought? Are analogies noted explicitly?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good hygiene: independent lines of evidence, recorded unsuccessful attempts, and explicit discussion of potential counterexamples. Poor hygiene: only cherry-picked confirming examples and silence about failed refutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori improbability principle (weighting confirmations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conjecture's plausibility increases more when verified consequences are less likely a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give special weight to confirmations of surprising or low-prior events — these are stronger evidence. Make explicit any background probabilities or expectations used informally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence principle (multiple independent confirmations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plausibility increases more when multiple independent consequences are verified than when dependent, redundant checks are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek diverse, independent lines of confirmation (different methods, different consequence types) and report their independence when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspicion when support restricted to special case
rubrics_metrics.description: A conjecture is suspect if its only support is restricted to a special case (i.e., it has not survived scrutiny across varied instances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report limitations of evidence candidly. If all evidence is from a narrow family of cases, qualify conclusions and avoid overgeneralizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge inductive evidence for conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should acknowledge the inductive evidence behind any conjecture they state — what was checked, what analogies or reductions motivated it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the basis of confidence: tested cases, analogous theorems, heuristic arguments. Transparency about inductive support helps readers evaluate plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish plausible reasoning from proof in exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present analogy-based suggestions or inductive support as if they were rigorous proofs; clearly mark conjectures and heuristic arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit language (conjecture, plausible, heuristic, suggested by analogy) versus theorem/proof. Readers should be able to tell what is proved and what is conjectured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt to refute conjectures before publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to publishing, attempt to refute your own conjectures — search for counterexamples and incompatible consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document refutation attempts and any partial negative evidence; active refutation-seeking strengthens the surviving conjectures' credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-generated math must include plausibility evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: An AI that generates mathematical claims should provide plausibility evidence (confirming cases, analogies, reductions) rather than just asserted proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing AI outputs, require explicit supporting evidence for conjectures: tested instances, analogical mappings, reductions. Treat bare assertions without evidence as suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI should respect distinction between conjecture and theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated tools must clearly label conjectures versus theorems and not conflate heuristic suggestion with formal proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce output formats that separate 'plausibility notes' from formal proofs; require provenance for both heuristic and deductive claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-patterns indicating low-quality mathematical work
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators of poor practice include confusing inductive evidence with proof, hiding analogies behind formalism, treating special-case exploration as embarrassing, asserting conjectures without indicating the basis of confidence, and failing to seek negative evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these anti-patterns as red flags in review: ask authors to add evidence, clarify analogies, report special-case findings, and describe refutation attempts before accepting claims at face value.
